summary: The builder can start: the DocumentDB MCP server and extensive documentdb_* skills are installed, Python is available, and Azure CLI is signed in. Key facts that a builder might assume from the model (resource type, CLI group, billing model, connection-string shape, local gateway and vector-index syntax) differ from the cold answers; the installed learn/documentdb MCP tools provide authoritative guidance and command examples. Missing accelerators and a few CLI tools (azd, bicep, terraform, mongosh) are optional but would speed development. The build is not blocked, but the implementer must follow the corrected facts below (resource type = Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, use az documentdb mongocluster commands, vCore billing model, integrated vector & full‑text search APIs, local gateway image on port 10260, etc.).
summary_points: All required runtime tools to write and run the Python LlamaIndex RAG sample are present (python, pip, docker, node, az, documentdb MCP server, documentdb skills).

Multiple cold answers were wrong or outdated: cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), CLI uses az documentdb mongocluster, and billing is compute+storage (vCore tiers), not RU/s.

Vector search and integrated full-text search are first-class features (HNSW, IVF, DiskANN) with documented createIndexes/createSearchIndexes templates — the model’s naive createIndex syntax is incorrect.
Local development: a DocumentDB Gateway Docker image exists (port 10260) — contrary to the cold answer that no emulator exists.
Missing but non-blocking accelerators: the DocumentDB Agent Kit aggregator is not installed (npx skills add ... would add it); CLI IaC tools (bicep, terraform, azd) are absent but optional.
No required MCP server or credential is missing; the build can proceed using the live cluster referenced by DOCUMENTDB_URI and the documentdb MCP server for verification.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (i.e. create a Cosmos DB "database account").
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB clusters the resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (the 'mongoClusters' resource). 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' is the Cosmos DB account resource used by legacy Cosmos SQL / RU-based accounts.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-03-01-preview (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services live under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider namespace historically; older Cosmos DB examples and the databaseAccounts resource are associated with Cosmos DB accounts and the Mongo API (RU) offering, whereas the newer vCore-managed clusters use a separate 'mongoClusters' resource.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses databaseAccounts resource types or ARM/Bicep snippets intended for databaseAccounts, they will produce control-plane IaC that targets the wrong resource type; provisioning or template examples may not apply to mongoClusters and could be rejected or mis-configured.
improvements: On Quickstarts and 'create cluster' docs: add a clear top-line: 'For vCore clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; do NOT use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for vCore clusters' (Quickstart: Create a cluster page).
Add a deprecation/clarification note on any 'databaseAccounts' page that references Mongo API to indicate when to use mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group in the core Azure CLI. Example: az cosmosdb create --name <account> --resource-group <rg> --kind MongoDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb (or az cosmosdb mongocluster) command group and specifically the mongocluster commands (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both legacy Cosmos DB examples (az cosmosdb) and the new mongoClusters commands sit in the Azure CLI; older quickstarts and docs use az cosmosdb for databaseAccounts. The product introduced dedicated 'documentdb mongocluster' commands for vCore clusters.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create with --kind MongoDB targets Cosmos DB databaseAccounts and RU-based provisioning, which is the wrong control-plane resource for vCore DocumentDB clusters; this could create the wrong account type or be rejected.
improvements: Update Azure CLI Quickstart pages to show az documentdb mongocluster commands first for vCore clusters and add a short note on when az cosmosdb examples are for RU-based Cosmos accounts.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" (provider azurerm) with kind = "MongoDB".
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed clusters use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (examples available for ARM/Bicep and Terraform AzAPI/AzVerified modules). databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account are for Cosmos DB accounts (RU-based).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-03-01-preview (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical overlap: Cosmos DB's databaseAccounts resource has been used for many Cosmos DB APIs (SQL, Mongo) and older tutorial code uses azurerm_cosmosdb_account; new vCore clusters are a separate resource family (mongoClusters) documented separately.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder writes IaC targeting databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account, it will not deploy the vCore mongoClusters resource (different resource schema and properties), causing provisioning failures if attempted.
improvements: In IaC Quickstarts and sample repos: include explicit examples for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM/Terraform AzAPI) and label them 'vCore DocumentDB (mongoClusters)'.
Add a one-line crosslink on databaseAccounts pages explaining when to use mongoClusters instead.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin. (Scheme mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// on SRV-supporting endpoints; host suffix .mongo.cosmos.azure.com, default TLS port 10255 for non-SRV endpoints; require ssl=true and often retryWrites=false and replicaSet=globaldb.)
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore DocumentDB mongoClusters the documented connection strings use modern Mongo URIs, often with mongodb+srv:// or mongodb+srv://<user>:<pwd>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/ and TLS (e.g., tls=true, authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256). The older .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 form is associated with Cosmos DB databaseAccounts/old Mongo API endpoints, not the mongoClusters SRV host names.

grounding_links.title: Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString-Description (examples showing mongodb+srv)
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB's older Mongo API used .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255; the new vCore mongoClusters use SRV-style hostnames and different host suffixes (.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and may return mongodb+srv connection strings. The shared 'Mongo' vocabulary caused the model to recall the older Cosmos pattern.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB account `[Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts]` (examples and legacy connection forms)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix and port (10255 and .mongo.cosmos.azure.com) may cause the application to fail to connect or to attempt a TLS/port combination that the cluster does not expose; SRV-style connection strings are the recommended shape for many mongoClusters.
improvements: In the Quickstart connection-string example, show both SRV (mongodb+srv) and non-SRV examples and add a clarifying sentence: 'If your cluster returns an SRV URI use that; older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts used .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255'.
Add a short example in 'how to connect' showing the exact parameters to set for pymongo (tls, authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256, retryWrites=false).

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model is Cosmos DB style throughput: provisioned RU/s (or autoscale RU/s) or serverless (RU consumption). There are also dedicated instance/compute tier offerings in some SKUs, but the standard model to plan for is RU/s (request units/sec) and serverless options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is billed by compute tier (vCores / named tiers like M30, M40) and provisioned storage; it is NOT billed by RU/s. RU-based throughput is the Cosmos DB (RU) model for the request-unit Cosmos offerings, which is a different SKU.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing model summary)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos DB' naming overlap and the historical Cosmos RU-based model cause the model to mix billing models—RU/s is the Cosmos RU account model, whereas the vCore DocumentDB offering bills compute/storage.
confusions.build_risk: Choosing RU-based code patterns or expecting RU autoscale would lead the implementer to the wrong control-plane and wrong capacity planning steps; cost estimates would be incorrect.
improvements: Add a short 'pricing model' banner on the product Overview/Quickstart pages: 'This product uses vCore tiers and per-shard storage billing; RU-based Cosmos DB accounts are a different offering.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API you authenticate with MongoDB-style credentials (database users / SCRAM username:password). The Cosmos account keys (primary/master keys) and resource tokens are used for Cosmos SQL API; Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication is not generally used for the MongoDB wire protocol endpoints. In short: use MongoDB user credentials (SCRAM) from the driver; Azure AD integration is for other Cosmos APIs and not the primary Mongo endpoint.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters support native Mongo-style authentication (SCRAM) and can be configured to allow Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication modes as an allowed data-auth mode on the cluster (auth-allowed-modes includes MicrosoftEntraID). The az CLI shows an --auth-allowed-modes flag allowing NativeAuth and MicrosoftEntraID.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create ( --auth-allowed-modes )

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically the Mongo endpoint relied on SCRAM credentials; newer vCore clusters added Microsoft Entra ID authentication as an allowed mode. The model recalled the historical default but missed the newer cluster auth mode option.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is unavailable they may implement insecure credential storage patterns or fail to request a recommended managed identity integration; conversely, assuming Entra ID without configuration will cause authentication failures.
improvements: Document the Microsoft Entra ID option on the 'connect' quickstart and in az documentdb mongocluster create examples with a sample --auth-allowed-modes setting and a short note how to configure driver-side MS Entra authentication.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For MongoDB API workloads use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. pymongo for Python, mongodb node driver). There is an azure-cosmos SDK but that is for the SQL/Core API — not for Mongo-compatible endpoints. So for this sample use pymongo / motor / official MongoDB drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo) and the LlamaIndex/LangChain integrations that rely on pymongo or the DocumentDB-specific vector store connectors. There is not a separate service-specific Mongo driver; applications should use MongoDB drivers.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python
Use LlamaIndex with Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: I expect provider-supported vector indexes include HNSW and IVF (and possibly DiskANN) exposed via an extended createIndex option. Example command I'd run (best-effort): db.patient_chunks.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {vector: {algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536, m:16, efConstruction:200}}). Note: this is an engine-specific extended createIndex syntax, not standard Mongo; you must supply the index type and parameters in the createIndex options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct in substance: Azure DocumentDB supports vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann. The documented creation pattern uses a createIndexes runCommand payload or a createIndexes template with cosmosSearchOptions, e.g. runCommand({"createIndexes":"coll","indexes":[{"key":{"contentVector":"cosmosSearch"},"cosmosSearchOptions":{"kind":"vector-hnsw","dimensions":1536,"similarity":"COS","m":16,"efConstruction":200}}]}) and queries use the $search stage with cosmosSearch.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector search examples)

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: There isn't a first-class MongoDB Atlas-style full-text/hybrid search built into the Mongo API; typical approach on Azure is to integrate with Azure Cognitive Search (indexing data via change feed or connectors). For vector+text hybrid search you either use the provider's vector indexes if available (see Q08) or export data into Azure Cognitive Search or an external vector search engine and perform hybrid ranking there.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: Azure DocumentDB includes integrated text search and vector search and provides a $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch) and createSearchIndexes/createIndexes patterns for text and vector indexes. Hybrid (BM25 + vector) workflows are supported via the $search/cosmosSearch stage and the createSearchIndexes facility — you do not need to move data to Azure Cognitive Search for hybrid search in this service.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (perform vector similarity search and textSearch guidance)
documentdb-full-text-search skill (installed)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model conflated older patterns (use Azure Cognitive Search as external search) with the new integrated vector/text search features of DocumentDB; community examples about external indexers influenced the memory.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder exported data to an external search service unnecessarily, they'd add extra infrastructure and operational burden and could miss more performant integrated queries with pre-filtering and BM25 hybrid techniques.
improvements: On the vector-search and full-text search docs: add a short 'hybrid search' example showing BM25 + vector retrieval in a single $search/cosmosSearch pipeline to discourage unnecessary externalization.
Surface the integrated $search examples high in the RAG/how-to pages rather than burying them.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect compatibility tiers that map to MongoDB server versions (commonly supported: 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4 and more recent accounts may advertise 5.x/6.x). Some MongoDB server features are limited or unsupported (server-side JavaScript, certain aggregation stages or operators, some admin commands, some transactional or change-stream behaviors depending on the compatibility level). Plan to verify the exact server version advertised by the account and test any advanced features you rely on.
confusions.grounded_answer: The service documents support for MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 (and in later docs 8.0 for supported clusters). There are feature differences compared to full MongoDB; DocumentDB documents a compatibility list and some administrative or lesser-used operators may not be supported. Builders should consult the 'compatibility' docs for exact operator coverage.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions supported)
MongoDB compatibility (operator support)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recalled older/more-conservative compatibility lists; the product now documents explicit support for more recent wire-protocol versions (5.x+).
confusions.build_risk: Assuming older protocol versions might lead a builder to add unnecessary compatibility layers or avoid using valid newer features, while assuming newer versions without checking could cause runtime incompatibilities.
improvements: Add a short 'supported wire protocol versions' section to connection/quickstart pages and show how to query the serverVersion property programmatically from the cluster to confirm.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no official Mongo API emulator for Cosmos that fully reproduces the managed service. For local development use a local MongoDB docker image (e.g. mongo:6.0) and bind port 27017. Example: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:6.0. Then point pymongo at mongodb://localhost:27017 for local testing.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is an official DocumentDB Gateway Docker image for local development: ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest (Gateway serving MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260). Local connection guidance (tls, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates, SCRAM-SHA-256) and docker-compose examples are provided in the documentdb-local-deployment guidance.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Local Gateway image (Gateway on port 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model generalized from Cosmos DB's historical lack of a faithful emulator and defaulted to using MongoDB's general docker image; it did not recall the DocumentDB project's provided Gateway Docker image and port 10260.
confusions.build_risk: Using a plain mongo:6.0 local image for integration tests can mask differences (vector search, createSearchIndexes, engine-specific behavior) and lead to tests that pass locally but fail against the real DocumentDB cluster.
improvements: Add a clear 'Local development' section on the main quickstart describing the Gateway Docker image and giving the exact docker-compose snippet (port 10260 and TLS guidance).
Ship a small docker-compose example in the sample repo that binds 10260 and documents SKIP_INIT_DATA/INIT_DATA_PATH.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API change streams historically were not fully supported; Cosmos DB has its own Change Feed mechanism on the SQL API. If you need change-stream-like behavior you either must use the provider's change feed API or verify that the account's MongoDB compatibility level explicitly advertises change stream support. In short: don't assume MongoDB change streams are available unless the specific account/compatibility level documents support for them.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams ARE supported for the MongoDB API and DocumentDB clusters; Microsoft documents change streams support and provides examples. Some limitations exist (e.g., delete events may not be supported or some properties like operationType/updateDescription may be limited); to use change streams you must ensure the account compatibility / server version supports them and follow the documented limitations.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure Cosmos DB’s API for MongoDB
Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically some Cosmos Mongo offerings had more limited change-stream behavior and the model recalled the conservative guidance; product docs have clarified support and limitations for change streams in Mongo API contexts.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are unsupported may lead the builder to implement inefficient polling or complex change-capture workarounds. Assuming full parity with MongoDB change streams without checking limitations (e.g., deleted events) may produce incorrect processing code.
improvements: On the change-streams page: show a succinct 'what's supported / not supported' table and an example of how to get shard-specific stream tokens (GetChangeStreamTokens) as documented.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (i.e. MCP server named "documentdb") for data-plane inspection tooling for this service. The general Azure MCP server does not provide the same Mongo/Cosmos-specific index/collection inspection commands; you need the documentdb-specific MCP server profile.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list databases, create/list indexes, aggregate, explain) specific to Azure DocumentDB; the azure MCP server covers control-plane Azure tasks but doesn't replace the documentdb data-plane toolset.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (installed in inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Originally Microsoft named the service DocumentDB; it was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB (Cosmos). The "MongoDB-compatible" surface is an API layer on top of the Cosmos engine. This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos service is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and from any unrelated open-source project called DocumentDB; they are separate implementations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but incomplete: The product was formerly referred to as vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB; it has been renamed/clarified as Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) to align with the open-source DocumentDB engine. It is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and from other Cosmos DB APIs. The open-source DocumentDB engine underpins Azure DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (naming and history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Naming history is complex: the term 'DocumentDB' previously referred to an older Azure service that became Cosmos DB; the new vCore offering inherited a similar name and was previously marketed as vCore-based Cosmos DB for MongoDB. This multi-stage rename causes models to conflate different historical names.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder cites older blog posts or samples that refer to 'DocumentDB' without context they may provision or target the wrong product or use obsolete examples.
improvements: Add a 'Naming timeline' section on the product 'Overview' page summarizing historical names and mapping them to the current product terms to avoid ambiguous references in docs and samples.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the Mongo-compatible surface sits the provider's proprietary storage/engine (Cosmos engine) that translates Mongo wire protocol operations into its internal operations. That means standard Mongo drivers usually work, but expect differences in supported commands, performance characteristics, consistency semantics, indexing behavior and some missing Mongo features. Application-level code should stick to widely-used driver APIs and test any advanced Mongo-specific features.
confusions.grounded_answer: The service is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the DocumentDB project) rather than the MongoDB server; the engine is open source and governed by the Linux Foundation. Application code still uses standard MongoDB drivers (wire-protocol compatible), but engine differences and supported operator lists are documented and should be checked.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (engine description)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model defaulted to 'proprietary Cosmos engine' phrasing (typical for Cosmos DB SQL API) instead of the up-to-date description that the vCore offering runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine. The similarity in names and overlapping marketing language caused the error.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a proprietary Cosmos engine (rather than DocumentDB) might lead to incorrect statements in readmes or incorrect assumptions about portability and licensing.
improvements: Document the engine (DocumentDB opensource) clearly on the product Overview and Quickstart pages and add a short 'what this means to applications' paragraph.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with HNSW params. Example I would run in the Mongo shell (engine-extended createIndex): db.patient_chunks.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_hnsw', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536, m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } });
confusions.grounded_answer: Create the vector index using the documented createIndexes/runCommand template with cosmosSearchOptions. Example (conceptual): runCommand({"createIndexes":"patient_chunks","indexes":[{"key":{"embedding":"cosmosSearch"},"cosmosSearchOptions":{"kind":"vector-hnsw","dimensions":1536,"similarity":"COS","m":16,"efConstruction":200}}]}) — the service uses cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions keys rather than a simple {embedding:'vector'} shape.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index creation templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model proposed a generic engine-extended createIndex variant; DocumentDB requires a specific createIndexes payload using the cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions naming.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues the naive createIndex call it will fail; the index creation must use the documented cosmosSearch options, and dimensions must match the embedding model.
improvements: Add a short, copy-paste code example in the quickstart that shows the exact runCommand createIndexes JSON for common vector index types (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) and dimension placeholder.

confusions.question: How do I create the application collection with patientId as the partition key / access-control key?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a collection named patient_chunks in database sample_healthcare_01 and ensure an index on patientId. Example (mongo shell): use sample_healthcare_01; db.createCollection('patient_chunks'); db.patient_chunks.createIndex({ patientId: 1 }); For sharded/partitioned Cosmos accounts you may also need to define the partition key at collection creation; in Mongo API this maps to ensuring patientId is the shard key.
confusions.grounded_answer: Create the collection and create an index on patientId; for sharded collections supply a shardKey at collection creation time (shardKey parameter in collection resource). In vCore clusters you may choose to shard the collection on patientId if you need multi-shard scale; otherwise keep single-shard and enforce patientId scoping at the app layer. The collection creation and shardKey parameter patterns are documented for the MongoDB collection resource.

Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases/collections (shardKey parameter)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model described the general Mongo createCollection / createIndex flow; on Azure you may need to pass shardKey/shard parameters at resource creation or use the service custom command for collection creation.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder relies only on createIndex without setting shardKey on a sharded cluster and then expects patientId to act as the partition key across shards, queries might be routed incorrectly or experience cross-shard overhead; app-level enforcement is still required for access control.
improvements: Add a short sample in the collection creation quickstart showing how to create a collection with shardKey patientId (both via az/documentdb mongocluster create or via the createCollection custom command) and a recommended default for sample apps (single-shard + app-scoped queries).

confusions.question: How should the Python app connect to the cluster reading DOCUMENTDB_URI?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo and read os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']. Example code: from pymongo import MongoClient; import os; uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']; client = MongoClient(uri, tls=True); db = client['sample_healthcare_01']; collection = db['patient_chunks']. Ensure the URI includes ssl=true and authSource=admin if required.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use pymongo and read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI (prefer mongodb+srv if provided). Example uses TLS (tls=true/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local) and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 if credentials are SCRAM-based. Keep the connection string secret and do not write it to logs.

confusions.question: What vector index creation command will the sample try to run to verify vector support?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample will attempt an engine-extended createIndex call like: db.patient_chunks.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_index', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536 } }); If that fails, fall back to storing embeddings and calling a provider-specific vector search API or external vector index.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the documented createIndexes/runCommand payload with cosmosSearchOptions (see S01). Example: runCommand({"createIndexes":"patient_chunks","indexes":[{"key":{"embedding":"cosmosSearch"},"cosmosSearchOptions":{"kind":"vector-hnsw","dimensions":1536,"similarity":"COS"}}]}); if createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions is rejected, the fallback is to store embeddings as arrays and run a brute-force kNN (client-side) or use an external vector index.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The example createIndex shape expected by the model is not the product's canonical createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions form.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting the wrong createIndex call will fail; implementers must use the documented createIndexes/runCommand shape or fall back to storing embeddings with client-side similarity compute.
improvements: Place the exact runCommand JSON in the sample repo and Quickstart so implementers can copy and run it verbatim.

confusions.question: How should we enforce patientId-based access control in this sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Enforce access control at the application layer: authenticate the requester (e.g. via your app's auth), then always add patientId equality to any query (e.g. collection.find({ patientId: allowed_patient_id, ...other_filters })). Do not rely on Mongo user-level per-document enforcement; instead use scoped queries and validate patientId on every operation. For admin tasks create a separate management user with broader rights.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: application-layer scoping is the recommended approach. The product docs and security guidance recommend enforcing patientId filters in every query, and not relying on per-document DB-level user separation. Use TLS and least-privilege admin users, and consider Private Endpoints/Entra RBAC for network/management access.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & dimension selection
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt asks to store embeddings but does not specify which embedding model (provider and exact model) to use; the docs do not pick a default. This matters because vector index 'dimensions' must match the embedding size. Looked in Microsoft Learn docs and the installed skills (documentdb-vector-search, LlamaIndex integrations) — they describe index param templates but do not mandate an embedding model or dimension.

information_gaps.title: LLM/chat model choice for clinical summarization
information_gaps.description: The prompt requests a clinical summary prompt-engineered for safety and context but does not specify the LLM provider or model (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, local LLM) or any safety/compliance guardrails. The installed skills show how to integrate with LlamaIndex but not which chat model to pick for clinical content. Looked in LlamaIndex integration docs and sample prompt review — no canonical model is mandated.

information_gaps.title: Seed data licensing and realistic clinical sample design
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks to include sample patient records but does not specify whether to use synthetic or real data or how to pseudonymize it. Docs/skills (documentdb-local-deployment) advise using synthetic data and SKIP_INIT_DATA patterns, but no canonical synthetic generator is provided in the installed skills or docs.

information_gaps.title: Exact recommended index parameter defaults for small samples
information_gaps.description: Skills describe tuning recommendations (e.g. HNSW m/ef, DiskANN lBuild/lSearch, IVF numLists) but do not provide a small-dataset 'default knobs' set to copy-paste for samples (dimensions aside). The vector-search docs give heuristics but the implementer must pick exact values.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the MongoClusters resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) and the az documentdb mongocluster CLI commands when discussing or automating vCore DocumentDB clusters; do NOT use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb create for vCore clusters.
Treat capacity as vCore/compute-tier + storage (e.g., M30), not RU/s; size the cluster by picking an M-tier and storage per shard, and document that RU-based Cosmos accounts are a separate offering.

Create vector indexes using the documented createIndexes/runCommand pattern with cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions (kind=vector-hnsw|vector-ivf|vector-diskann) and set dimensions to your embedding model's output size; do not use a naive {embedding:'vector'} createIndex call.
